Three views are drawn: a plan view and a sectioned profile view showing the fuel cells, the Step I, II and III oxidiser and fuel tanks, liquid oxygen and liquid nitrogen for the environmental control system, parachute storage, the ascent engine blast tube, the docking radar, the landing gear and its shock attenuation and the extended airlock; and beneath them a plan view of the living area labelled with the laboratory work and storage areas, food storage and preparation, a portable eating table, a sofa or bunk, personal gear storage, a shower, a lavatory and a waste station.

Figure 30 of the Aeronutronic study, the inboard profile of MEM configuration D8-1, the canted lander that was not chosen. The vehicle is drawn nose-high on a nose leg and two main legs, sectioned to show the command module separation joint, the docking window and radar, the fuel cells, the Step I, II and III propellant tanks, the ascent engine, the living area and its access door, the airlock and parachute storage, with a separate plan view of the living area naming the laboratory work and storage area, an eating area, a relief station, lavatories, a shower and a sofa or bunk.

Figure 26 of the Aeronutronic study, the general arrangement of the tail sitter vehicle: a dimensioned outline of the half-cone lifting body in rear and side view, marked 400 inches across the two winglets, 264 inches across the body, 360 inches long, with a 164 inch radius and a 49.2 inch spherical nose radius.

Figure 9 of Gordon Woodcock's June 1966 memorandum, the Mars Excursion Module concept: a labelled section through the Apollo-cone lander showing the separable cap, the 4 man cabin with a viewport and a floating astronaut, the egress lock, the ascent stage with its LOX tank, super insulation and a pressurant gas helium sphere, the descent stage carrying the Mars surface operations crew quarters and the landing propellant, the ascent stage propulsion and the landing engines, the thrust structure and the heat shield. The paragraph of body text above the figure is part of the scanned page.

A 1969 Marshall Space Flight Center cutaway painting headed MARS EXCURSION MODULE CONFIGURATION and numbered MSFC-69 PD-SA 164, showing an Apollo-shaped Mars Excursion Module landed on a red plain with its ramp down, a surface vehicle and crew quarters in the lower body, a ladder, the ascent stage on the centreline and an astronaut in the cabin at the top of the cone.

missions.name: Mars Surveyor 2001 Lander
missions.status: Built and never flown: NASA said on 28 March 2000 that it was cancelled and on hold indefinitely, a near copy of Mars Polar Lander, which had crashed on 3 December 1999. Its structure reached Mars in 2008 as Phoenix.

images.alt: A colour photograph of a Mars Surveyor 2001 lander standing on three white test stands in a bare high-bay cell, its circular equipment deck wrapped in gold and silver thermal blanketing with amber plumbing and cabling running across it, protective yellow tape and red covers on the deck edge, and camera tripods and ground support cabling on the floor around it. JPL published it in a gallery headed ATLO Test and Integration Images on the lander's own site, with no individual caption and no date.

A close colour photograph taken under the rim of the lander deck, showing gold multilayer insulation folded back over tanks and lines, a cluster of small rocket nozzles pointing down at the centre of the frame, valve and connector blocks bolted to the underside, and white cable harness taped across the structure. It is one of four frames JPL published without captions in the ATLO Test and Integration Images gallery.

A labelled computer rendering of the 2001 lander's science deck seen from above and to one side, with white pointer arrows naming the Martian Radiation Environment Experiment (MARIE), Mini-TES, the APEX Pancam on its mast, the Mars In Situ Propellant Production experiment (MIP), the Mars Environmental Compatibility Assessment (MECA) and a Mossbauer Spectrometer, with two solar panels and the rover deployment ramp cut off at the edges of the frame. The rendering was made for the mission website, and the page that carries it credits the site's 2001 artwork to Corby J. Waste of JPL.

Museum object photography of the Marie Curie rover on its black plinth at the National Air and Space Museum, three-quarter view from the front left, showing the black solar panel with its colour calibration targets along the edge, the gold-foiled warm electronics box, the rocker-bogie suspension and all six cleated aluminium wheels. Part of the plinth label reading SOJOURNER FLIGHT SPARE MARIE C is visible at bottom left.

The Marie Curie rover as displayed at the National Air and Space Museum, standing on a pink plinth against a painted Martian backdrop with a larger rover model behind it. The exhibit label in the foreground is headed Marie Curie Rover, Sojourner's Flight Spare, and its text records that Sojourner landed on 4 July 1997 and operated for 85 days, that the rover shown is Sojourner's flight spare, and that the object was transferred from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

A colour photograph released by JPL as PIA01885, showing the Phoenix Mars Lander partway through assembly and testing at Lockheed Martin Space Systems in Denver in September 2006, the lander deck on a work fixture in the clean room with its two circular solar arrays unfolded flat on either side and three gowned technicians working over the deck.

missions.name: Mars Telecommunications Orbiter
missions.status: Cancelled on 21 July 2005 before construction, and nothing replaced it. NASA sought proposals for a commercially built Mars Telecommunications Network on 14 May 2026, with no award announced as of 24 August 2026.

images.alt: The JPL artist's concept released on 29 March 2005 as PIA07500, titled Mars Telecommunications Orbiter, Artist's Concept, showing the spacecraft in front of Mars with a gold-blanketed bus, a large white high-gain dish, two long solar wings, a cylindrical optical terminal assembly on top and a flat radiator panel below.

The JPL artist's concept released on 29 March 2005 as PIA07499, titled Mars Laser Communication Demonstration, Artist Concept, showing the Mars Telecommunications Orbiter above Mars with a red beam running from the small optical terminal on its upper deck all the way to Earth. NASA's caption describes it as a concept for operation of an optical communications system on the orbiter, with the primary work left to the radio link.

A JPL graphic released on 29 November 2016 as PIA21139, Strengthening the Mars Telecommunications Network, showing the geometry of the rover Opportunity transmitting UHF data up to ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter, whose long elliptical orbit is drawn in red around the planet. The orbiter received the data on one of its NASA-supplied Electra UHF radios and relayed it to Earth on its own X-band link.

missions.name: Mars Life Explorer
missions.status: Still a concept as of 24 August 2026, with no new start, funding line or launch date. The 2022 decadal survey made this ice-drilling lander NASA's top medium-class Mars mission, to follow sample return's peak spending.

images.alt: An artist's concept of the Mars Life Explorer standing on rocky ground under a pale orange sky: a lander in the Phoenix and InSight mould, with two circular fan-fold solar arrays spread either side, instrument boxes on the deck, and a tall vertical drill mast reaching down to the surface beside the leg. The Planetary Society captions it as the Mars Life Explorer operating on the surface with its drill deployed. Nothing has been built.

A HiRISE excerpt from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing a small fresh impact crater in the northern mid-latitudes, a bright white patch of excavated ice at its centre surrounded by a dark blast scar on rippled orange ground, with a 100 metre scale bar. NASA's record states that the impact exposed bright ice that had been hidden just beneath the surface at this location.

The Subsurface Water Ice Mapping map, a grey shaded-relief Mars base with the Tharsis volcanoes and Valles Marineris across the lower half and a broad blue wash covering the northern plains, marking where NASA missions have detected subsurface water ice. Triangles are past and present landed missions, circles are ice-exposing impact craters. NASA's record states that the project mapped from the equator to 60 degrees north, hunting ice in the mid-latitudes: far enough toward the pole for water ice to be plentiful, but close enough to the equator to avoid the coldest temperatures on Mars.

missions.name: ARES, the Mars airplane
missions.status: Never built beyond subscale test articles. NASA Langley's rocket-powered aeroplane, designed for a single 70-minute flight over the Southern Highlands, lost Mars Scout to Phoenix in 2003 and was passed over in 2007.

images.alt: Roughly fifty members of the ARES team in matching blue ARES polo shirts, packed shoulder to shoulder around a full-scale ARES test airplane indoors at NASA Langley, the aircraft finished in white with dark blue sweeps and a United States flag on its tail fin. The Commons file page identifies team leader Joel S. Levine at the bottom right. This airframe is a ground test article built at Langley, and no ARES was ever built to go to Mars.

The half-scale ARES drop-test aircraft, which the project called the Mars Eagle, sitting on a wooden cradle on a fog-bound airfield apron with its wings and tail deployed, white with orange wingtips and tail, cables trailing across the tarmac, and a Douglas DC-3 parked behind it. The project's multimedia page captions the frame as the ARES Mars Eagle on the morning of the high altitude drop test with a DC-3 in the background.

A frame from the tail-mounted video camera of the half-scale Mars Eagle during its 19 September 2002 high-altitude flight, looking forward along a deployed wing and the twin tail booms towards a black sky and the curved bright limb of the Earth, with cloud and terrain far below. The project's multimedia page captions it as the ARES Mars Eagle descending over Oregon during its high altitude flight test.

A bare metal ARES wind-tunnel model mounted upside down on a yellow-taped sting inside NASA Langley's Transonic Dynamics Tunnel, wings and tail in their fully deployed positions, rows of pressure taps drilled into the wing, tunnel lights burning through portholes in the wall behind it. The project's multimedia page captions the frame as the current ARES wind tunnel model in the TDT in May 2004.

The entry, descent and deployment figure from the 2006 ARES proposal documentation. Four CAD panels across the top show the folded airplane still inside the backshell at heat shield release, the release pyros firing, extraction complete on the drogue riser, and the wings deploying beneath the supersonic parachute. Below them an altitude against downrange plot traces the whole sequence with three sigma Monte Carlo boxes, and a table lists every event from atmospheric interface at 135 km and Mach 24 to pullout complete at 2.41 km and Mach 0.64, 309 seconds later. It is an engineering drawing of a vehicle that was never built.

A NASA Langley artist's concept of the drogue chute and tail deployment step, drawn over cratered Martian highlands. A dark truss, the airplane extraction structure, hangs beneath the white drogue canopy at the upper left with its own risers running up out of frame; a single line runs down from the canopy to the aircraft, and the aircraft itself is shown with its tail unfolded but its wings still folded flat down against the fuselage. The backshell is not in frame. The project's own multimedia page labels this image an artist's concept of ARES during drogue chute and tail deployment.

missions.name: Hera at Deimos
missions.status: Success: Hera photographed the far side of Deimos from about 1,000 km on 12 March 2025 during a Mars gravity assist. In August 2026 those frames pinned a Nature Astronomy reconstruction to a 320 m impactor.

images.alt: Deimos as a dark, irregular silhouette against the brighter disc of Mars, in a monochrome visible-light frame from Hera's 1020 by 1020 pixel Asteroid Framing Camera taken during the gravity assist of 12 March 2025 from about 1,000 km. ESA's caption places the bright Terra Sabaea region at the top, part of the 450 km Huygens crater at the right and part of Hellas Basin at the bottom right.

The same encounter in mid-infrared, from the Thermal Infrared Imager that JAXA supplied to Hera. Deimos is the small bright spot below the centre of a cooler Mars, because the airless, very dark moon absorbs sunlight and heats up while Mars is more reflective and moves heat around with its atmosphere. Hellas Basin is the cool purple region at the lower right, and a brightness temperature scale runs down the right-hand edge.

A near-infrared frame from HyperScout H, Hera's hyperspectral imager, which works in 25 visible and near-infrared bands to characterise surface materials. Mars is rendered pale blue and Deimos appears as a small dark ellipse in front of it, with Terra Sabaea at the top, the Huygens and 460 km Schiaparelli craters below it and Hellas Basin at the lower right.

A stereo pair of Deimos built from Hera's 12 March 2025 flyby frames by Sir Brian May of the Hera science team, published by ESA on 14 August 2026. A dashed white circle on the right-hand frame marks one of the ancient impact depressions lying under the moon's regolith blanket. Sabina Raducan says these buried features were not obvious by eye in the flat images and that the stereo rendering is what revealed them, supplying the last constraint on her Nature Astronomy reconstruction.

ESA's briefing graphic of 10 March 2025, published two days before the flyby. It gives Deimos a maximum diameter of 12.4 km and an orbit 20,068 km above the Martian surface, states that the trajectory brings Hera within 300 km of the moon while the three instruments will image it from a minimum of 1,000 km, labels the Asteroid Framing Camera, HyperScout H and the JAXA-supplied Thermal Infrared Imager on a drawing of the spacecraft, and sets Deimos beside the 780 m Didymos and the 151 m Dimorphos.

missions.name: Red Dragon
missions.entity: SpaceX with NASA Ames Research Center (United States)
missions.status: Cancelled on 19 July 2017, when Musk dropped propulsive landing for Dragon: the capsule was to land on Mars on its own engines with no parachute, announced by SpaceX on 27 April 2016. None was ever built.

images.alt: SpaceX concept art titled Dragon to Mars, showing a Dragon capsule glowing white hot as it enters the martian atmosphere at hypersonic speed, dragging a long incandescent wake across the sunlit face of the planet with the canyon system of Valles Marineris below it.

SpaceX concept art of a Dragon 2 capsule a few metres above the martian surface with its four landing legs extended, SuperDraco engines firing from the pods set into its side walls and blasting grit horizontally across the ground.
SpaceX concept art of a landed Dragon capsule standing alone on its legs in a wide rock-strewn martian valley, small against the ridges and the dusty horizon.

SpaceX concept art of a Falcon Heavy with a Dragon capsule on top climbing away from launch complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in a bank of exhaust, posted to the Official SpaceX Photos Flickr account on 27 April 2016, the day SpaceX announced it would send Dragons to Mars as early as 2018.

missions.name: International Mars Ice Mapper
missions.entity: NASA, CSA, JAXA and ASI, later joined by the Netherlands Space Office
missions.status: NASA terminated its financial support on 28 March 2022 and the other partners did not follow: Italy signed a 22 million euro Phase B1 contract on 8 March 2024. As of 24 August 2026 no agency has said whether it lives.

images.alt: NASA's artist illustration of the International Mars Ice Mapper, published with the 3 February 2021 announcement of the statement of intent. The radar orbiter is in the foreground low over Mars with its solar wings out and a large mesh reflector carried above it on a boom, a wedge shaped radar swath cutting down into the ground below it, and three smaller relay orbiters strung out higher up with a beam running to Earth at the top right. NASA's own file metadata captions it as four orbiters that are part of the I-MIM mission.

JAXA's own chart of its Strategic Mars Exploration Program, published with its 3 March 2021 statement on the Mars Ice Mapper agreement. A grey arrow curves from the 2020s at the lower left, through Martian Moons Exploration and its objectives, up through a Small Orbiter and EDL Demonstration box captioned Distribution and Inventory of Water with an inset picture of MIM beside it, on to lander and rover exploration in the 2030s captioned Evolution of Water, and finally to multiple and sustainable Mars exploration at 20xx.

A global map of buried water ice on Mars released by JPL on 10 December 2019, made by combining data from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Odyssey and Mars Global Surveyor. Colour gives the depth to ice over a grey shaded relief base, from magenta at less than about 10 cm to red at more than 80 cm; the black areas are ground where a landing spacecraft would sink into fine dust, and the white outlined box in the northern mid latitudes marks the region JPL calls ideal for sending astronauts who need to dig up water ice.

missions.name: Idefix (MMX Phobos rover)
missions.entity: CNES and DLR, flying with JAXA
missions.status: Launched on 20 October 2026, stowed on JAXA's MMX, which lifted off at 04:41:03 Japan time (19:41:03 UTC on 19 October) on H3 flight 10. Release onto Phobos from 40 to 100 metres up follows in late 2028 or early 2029.

images.alt: The Idefix flight rover in its cruise configuration, published by ISAS with the caption 'IDEFIX Rover' alongside the 14 March 2024 announcement of the handover to JAXA at the Mitsubishi Electric Kamakura Works. The body is wrapped in gold and black thermal blanketing, two of its four wheels are folded flat against the flank facing the camera on their stowed hinged legs, and the top face carries the orange-red blanket over the folded solar panels studded with the open aluminium lattice crash pads that take the impact when the rover is dropped. It sits in a handling frame on protective sheeting, with a Centre National d'Etudes Spatiales label visible on the wall behind.

Idefix in its stowed position on the MMX spacecraft at the Tanegashima Space Center, captioned by CNES as 'Insertion of an SD card inside Idefix®'. The rover is bolted to a spacecraft panel amid gold multi-layer insulation and black structure, red thermal blanket over its folded solar panels, lattice crash pads standing proud, wheels folded against its sides, while an engineer in cleanroom coveralls works at an opened flap on its upper face. Parts of the background are deliberately blurred in the frame CNES published.

A close-up of one folded wheel of the Idefix rover, photographed on 7 September 2023 in a cleanroom, showing the machined mesh-like wheel disc and the curved blades or grousers around its rim. The photographer's own caption describes the rover as folded and ready for flight before its transfer to Japan, and says the view focuses on a wheel with its special pads for moving on a soft Phobos surface.

Prototypix, the Earth prototype of Idefix, on the Phobos-analogue yard of DLR's Planetary Exploration Laboratory at Oberpfaffenhofen near Munich, during the four-day test campaign of late November 2025. The dark-bodied prototype carries DLR, CNES and JAXA markings, stands on four bright metal wheels with two of them lifted so the body is tilted back, and grooved wheel tracks run across the grey regolith simulant around it. Engineers watch from behind a rail at the edge of the yard. CNES's own caption reads 'Prototypix tests out the heliotropic sequence' and adds that the prototype is not hailing the Sun.

A figure from the rover team's own 2025 paper showing the autonomous uprighting sequence. The upper part is a schematic of the named body positions the rover moves through, Cruise, Parachutist, Flat, Inverse stowed, Stowed and Dragster, linked by coloured arrows with 'four legs at a time' on two of the transitions and a red branch marked 'If global Blockage counter is 8 or more'. The lower strip is four frames of the same manoeuvre rendered in a simulated environment, ending with the solar panels open. Every frame is either a diagram or a simulation.

A frame from DLR's physics simulation of the rover driving on Phobos, captioned by DLR as 'The MMX Rover moving on Phobos (simulation)'. The vehicle is shown deployed, solar panels spread on both sides, wheels on the ground, with a shallow track behind it across a grey boulder-strewn surface under a black sky. The image carries a DLR Robotics and Mechatronics Center and Institute of System Dynamics and Control watermark at the top left and a simulation clock reading 'Time: 764.7200s' at the bottom left.

missions.name: Mangalyaan-2 (Mars Lander Mission)
missions.status: Announced in October 2014 and still unfunded: the Space Commission approved it in February 2025, and the Union Cabinet, which releases the money, had not by 24 August 2026. No Mars window opens in 2030.

images.alt: Dr V. Narayanan seated at ISRO Headquarters in Bengaluru on 15 January 2025, the day ISRO announced he had begun functioning there, beneath the State Emblem of India and the wall lettering 'Government of India, Department of Space, ISRO Headquarters' in English and Hindi. The frame carries ISRO's own on-screen caption naming him Secretary, Department of Space and Chairman, ISRO.

An LVM3 lifting off from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, on the LVM3-M5 mission carrying the CMS-03 communications satellite on 2 November 2025. The vehicle is caught at the instant of lift-off with its two solid strap-on boosters burning, still level with the swing arms of the service structure and flanked by both lightning towers, and the SDSC SHAR sign is visible at the base.

missions.name: Aeolus and the Relativity Mars orbiter
missions.status: Announced on 17 June 2026 and still undisclosed in almost every detail: NASA supplies the four-instrument Aeolus payload, Relativity pays for and flies the orbiter. Launch is 2028 on Terran R, which has never flown.

images.alt: A Relativity Space computer render of the company's proposed Mars orbiter, a compact boxy bus carrying two long multi-panel solar wings, coasting in front of a fully lit Mars.

A photograph of NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman announcing the public-private partnership at Relativity Space on 17 June 2026, addressing a large seated and standing crowd on the factory floor with a United States flag and a long Relativity-branded rocket stage lying horizontally behind him.

missions.name: Space Reactor-1 Freedom
missions.status: Announced on 24 March 2026 for a December 2028 launch: it would be the first spacecraft to propel itself beyond Earth orbit on a fission reactor. By August 2026 it had a requirements-level review and no rocket.

images.alt: NASA's artist's concept of Space Reactor-1 Freedom passing Mars, showing the two large solar wings of the Gateway Power and Propulsion Element, a long truss boom carrying the reactor and its radiators, and the blue plume of an electric thruster firing.

NASA's Space Reactor-1 Freedom Flight Path graphic, plotting the SR-1 trajectory against the orbits of Earth and Mars and numbering seven events: launch in late 2028, solar array deployment at one day, reactor startup at 30 days, a first Mars flyby at 300 days, release of the SkyFall capsule at 600 days, and a second Mars flyby and atmospheric entry at 660 days.

A cleanroom photograph of Gateway's Power and Propulsion Element undergoing battery installation at Lanteris Space Systems in Palo Alto, California, showing the flight bus on its handling fixture with multi-layer insulation, orange cabling and a painted United States flag on its side.

missions.name: SkyFall
missions.status: Adopted by NASA on 24 March 2026, cut from AeroVironment's six-helicopter concept to three: released in mid-air with no lander involved. Launch is December 2028 aboard SR-1 Freedom, landing in autumn 2030.

images.alt: A NASA artist's concept of the SkyFall manoeuvre, seen from below, with three small helicopters flying away from the aeroshell while it still hangs beneath its inflated parachute in the Martian atmosphere.

NASA image PIA26760, an artist's concept of the three SkyFall helicopters working over Martian ground, with green cones drawn beneath their antennas to represent ground-penetrating radar sounding and red beams to represent near-infrared imaging of the regolith.

The banner still from AV's Skyfall reveal, showing a helicopter flying clear of the capsule as it descends under its parachute, with the words ARTIST'S CONCEPT printed in the top right corner by the company.

missions.name: The Impulse and Relativity Mars lander
missions.status: Dormant rather than cancelled: announced on 19 July 2022 for a launch as soon as late 2024, moved to 2026 in May 2023, and unmentioned by either company since. No hardware, customer or payload has ever been shown.

images.alt: An Impulse Space render of the Mars Cruise Vehicle, a small spacecraft with two black solar panels, flying beside the released entry capsule and its blunt heat shield above a mostly sunlit Mars, with the night side falling away at the left limb.
An Impulse Space render of the proposed Mars lander, a four-legged vehicle descending on two engines through a dust-coloured Martian sky with the ground faintly visible below.
